item.title: China's consumption shifts toward smart, health-related products: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market showed a stronger move toward smart, health-related and higher-quality products in the first eight months of 2026, with sales of smart glasses on major platforms surging 120 percent year on year, the Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday. Sales of electrocardiogram monitors jumped 75 percent during this period, while those of action cameras and organic food rose 26.9 percent and 7.4 percent, respectively, according to an official with the ministry. The latest breakdown offers a closer look at changes within China's consumer market after official data revealed that the combined retail sales of goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year in the January-August period. Demand also remained robust for a range of consumption-upgrade products. Sales of communication equipment increased 16.3 percent, while cosmetics items registered growth of 6.1 percent, and sales of cultural products and office supplies were up by 6 percent. In contrast, sales of petroleum products fell 6.1 percent year on year in this period, which the official partly attributed to substitution by new-energy products. Services continued to outpace goods consumption. Retail sales of services expanded 4.9 percent in the first eight months of 2026, 3.9 percentage points faster than retail sales of goods. Demand for tourism consulting and rental services, as well as cultural, sports and leisure services, maintained relatively rapid growth during the summer holiday season, as Chinese consumers increasingly spent on services alongside physical goods, according to the official. Consumption growth also continued to spread beyond major cities. Rural retail sales of consumer goods reached 4.4 trillion yuan (about 651.65 billion U.S. dollars), up 2.3 percent year on year, and 1.3 percentage points faster than the growth recorded in urban areas. Boosting consumption remains a policy priority for China this year. In July, China unveiled a five-year plan for expanding consumption, outlining measures to upgrade both goods and services consumption and expand quality services in areas including catering, tourism, elderly care and healthcare. China has also expanded policy support for smart and energy-efficient consumption. Under its 2026 consumer goods trade-in program, backed by ultra-long special treasury bonds, subsidies cover automobiles, six categories of home appliances and four types of digital and smart products. Smart glasses were included among the nationally subsidized digital and smart products for 2026, with eligible purchases receiving subsidies of 15 percent of the sales price, capped at 500 yuan per item. ■

item.title: China's five-year plan to elevate electronic information manufacturing sector
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly significant role in reshaping the global industrial landscape, China has recently unveiled a plan to advance its electronic information manufacturing sector, a critical foundation for AI development, over the next five years. The development plan for the electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the National Development and Reform Commission, aims to further consolidate the pillar role of the industry by 2030. Industrial firms in the sector with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) are expected to see their combined revenue surpass 30 trillion yuan, and R&D investment intensity of the sector will rise to 3.5 percent, according to the plan. TO ENHANCE INDUSTRIAL BASE The electronic information manufacturing industry is a major force in the new industrialization drive. By the end of 2025, China's electronic information manufacturing industry had led the country's 41 major industrial sectors in terms of revenue for 13 consecutive years. Building on that foundation, the plan presents a systemic framework to strengthen the industrial base, spanning integrated circuits, electronic components and materials, intelligent sensors, specialized electronic equipment and measuring instruments, and the photonics industry. The framework aims to tackle bottlenecks in key areas and build an independent and controllable industrial base, said Liu Bin, an official with the MIIT. Liu pointed to photonics as an example, noting that advancing breakthroughs in core technologies and establishing pilot testing platforms for key areas and shared needs will strengthen the sector from the ground up. These efforts, he said, will lay a solid foundation for development and accelerate both technological innovation and industrialization process. As a representative sector of the electronic information manufacturing industry, China's integrated circuit industry is entering a new phase of rapid growth, driven by the explosive global demand for high-end computing and memory chips brought about by the AI revolution. Customs data shows that in the first seven months, the country's integrated circuit exports reached 216 billion U.S. dollars, up 99.5 percent year on year, already surpassing the full-year total of 2025. A semiconductor technology company in southwest China's Sichuan Province has already completed its first half-year production targets, and aims to double its output value from last year, according to its general manager. TO STRENGTHEN COMPETITIVENESS While strengthening the industrial base, the plan also sets out strategies to boost the competitiveness of whole devices and systems. This includes enhancing industrial chain resilience in key areas, developing a robust computing ecosystem, and promoting innovation in consumer electronics, among other initiatives. Terminals form the basic foundation of industrial scale and serve as the gateway through which smart technologies reach hundreds of millions of users, said Liang Linjun, a researcher at China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT). The plan outlines a dedicated push for innovation in key consumer electronics products, ranging from high-end mobile phones and personal computers to virtual reality devices. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), China's output of core consumer electronics, including mobile phones and computers, maintained a top global ranking. The accelerating evolution of a new generation of AI is bringing new demand, new product forms, and new ways of development to the electronic information manufacturing industry, while raising higher requirements for basic hardware supply and system coordination, said Liang. Liang called for efforts to open up typical application scenarios, develop standards for agent collaboration, high-speed computing interconnect, and hardware-software compatibility, increase long-term capital supply that matches innovation cycles, and train more talent with expertise in both AI and electronics manufacturing. The plan also addresses rising concerns over cutthroat competition in the industry. It calls for timely revisions to industry norms, coordinated planning and early-warning systems for capacity across subsectors, and a comprehensive effort to curb cutthroat competition. As the "hardware foundation" of the digital world, the electronic information manufacturing industry is undergoing profound changes in its strategic position, competitive logic, and growth model, said Ao Li, vice president of the CAICT. Turning scale into systemic strength, as well as moving from leading in volume to winning on quality, will be a major task for China's electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Ao said. Industry insiders say government, industry, academia, research institutions, and users need to work together to translate the plan into results by strengthening the industrial foundation and making the supply chain more resilient. Such a collective push is expected to put China's electronic information manufacturing sector on firmer footing, with a more complete chain and more active innovation, and to lay a solid base for the country's goals of building itself into a manufacturing powerhouse and a cyber powerhouse, they said. ■

item.title: China's Global Development Initiative gives Global South stronger voice, opportunities: former Egyptian PM
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
CAIRO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's Global Development Initiative (GDI) helps give developing countries, especially those in the Global South, a stronger voice in global governance while creating broader opportunities for development, former Egyptian Prime Minister Essam Sharaf has said. "After decades of major economic and social transformation, China has accumulated considerable development experience and become more willing to share this experience and its capabilities with other countries, especially those of the Global South," Sharaf, founder and chairman of the Sharaf Foundation for Sustainable Development, told Xinhua in a recent interview. Sharaf said one of the GDI's most important contributions over the past five years has been to bring development back to "the heart of global attention" at a time of geopolitical conflicts, economic competition and successive crises. "Development should not become a victim of these conflicts, but should remain a shared priority for the international community," he stressed, noting that peace and development are closely intertwined. Sharaf said sustainable peace is difficult to build in a world where development gaps are widening, just as real development is difficult to achieve amid conflict and instability. "One of the most important lessons reinforced by the initiative is that investing in development is, at the same time, an investment in stability, peace and the future," he said. Sharaf said the GDI also reflects a broader understanding of development that goes beyond economic growth and new projects to improve people's livelihood, reduce poverty, ensure access to food and energy, and strengthen health, education and resilience to crises. Turning to global governance, Sharaf said the GDI contributes to strengthening multilateralism by promoting greater participation of developing countries in international decision-making. "From this perspective, I believe the GDI makes an important contribution to shifting from the concept of governance for countries to a broader concept of governance with the participation of countries," Sharaf said. He said that the GDI's emphasis on participation is particularly important because major global challenges, from climate change and food security to energy and digital transformation, cannot be addressed by any single country alone. "Ultimately, true multilateralism is not simply about having a large number of countries around one table; it is about ensuring that everyone feels they have a voice, and that their interests and needs are part of the process of shaping a shared future," Sharaf said. He expected the digital sphere to be one of the most important areas for the GDI's future development, as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly central to one of the fastest technological transformations in human history. Sharaf warned that if advanced technologies are available only to wealthier countries and societies, the world could move from the traditional development gap to an even more dangerous digital divide. He said supporting the "Digital South" should go beyond expanding internet access and digital infrastructure to include building human capacity, transferring knowledge, strengthening digital education and scientific research, and ensuring equitable access to technology. Sharaf said the GDI can play an important role in linking digital development with equitable development, while helping ensure that developing countries benefit from advances in artificial intelligence. He also pointed to the China-led establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, saying it aims to strengthen international cooperation and global AI governance while promoting the safe, equitable and inclusive development and use of artificial intelligence. "I believe the GDI has a major opportunity to help shape an important principle for the next phase: the future of technology should not be a future for a limited number of countries, but a shared future for humanity," he said.■

item.title: Border highway unlocks new growth along China's frontier
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
CHANGCHUN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- In early autumn, Chen Mo, a self-driving tourist from Hangzhou, pulled into a themed rest stop along National Highway G331 in northeast China's Jilin Province. Setting off from Dandong in neighboring Liaoning Province, he planned a seven-day journey along the border road to Hunchun in Jilin, hoping to experience Korean ethnic customs, pick local mountain produce and take in the riverside scenery along the way. "I used to think border areas were just places to pass through," Chen said. "Now, they are worth staying for." Stretching 1,240 km across Jilin, G331 runs along the province's border, skirting the Changbai Mountains and tracing the Yalu and Tumen rivers. The route passes through 10 county-level areas and links 216 border villages, 12 border ports and 45 scenic attractions rated AAA level or above. Parts of the route were once narrow, winding and difficult to navigate, making many border villages and attractions hard to reach. After years of upgrades, the Jilin section fully opened to traffic in September 2025 and has since drawn a growing stream of travelers to the region. During the 2025 Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday -- the first major holiday after the road opened -- traffic volume along the route topped 307,000, up 410.82 percent year on year, with a daily peak of 50,100. Ji'an, the first stop in Jilin for travelers arriving from Liaoning along the route, was once a key departure point for the Chinese People's Volunteers as they crossed the Yalu River to fight in the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea (1950-1953). The city boasts a wealth of revolutionary sites, many of which once lay off the beaten track. Now, the G331 is bringing these areas within easier reach for tourists. The city has renovated historic sites, upgraded study trails and improved visitor services, linking them with border landmarks to create routes that combine revolutionary history, border sightseeing and self-driving travel. "I brought my child here by car to experience history firsthand," said visitor Wang Junjun. "Seeing the border landscape and the Yalu River up close made the trip both meaningful and memorable." At the eastern end of G331's Jilin section, Hunchun is seeing another type of longer stay. The city, Jilin's only land-port city open to Russia, has attracted more Russian visitors as travel between the two countries has become easier under visa-free policies. Passenger traffic through Hunchun Port reached a record high of 754,000 in 2025. Traditional Chinese medicine and wellness services are becoming a particular draw for Russian visitors. Acupuncture, moxibustion and massage are among the treatments gaining popularity, with some visitors shifting from brief trips to longer wellness stays and opting for short-term therapy lasting seven to 10 days. "I was worried about the language barrier, but everything went smoothly," said a visitor from St. Petersburg after an acupuncture session in Hunchun. "The doctor also showed me some simple stretches I could do at home." The growing flow of visitors is also creating opportunities for local residents. An Guangri, a retired soldier in Fangchuan Village in Hunchun, converted an idle farmhouse into a border-themed homestay. "Since the highway opened, we've seen more self-driving tourists, as well as visitors from Russia and the Republic of Korea," he said, adding that during the peak season, rooms are often booked two weeks in advance. For Wu Meihong, the changes along G331 offered her a reason to come home. She returned to Qushui Village in Tumen in 2023 and, with her sister, renovated an unused old house into a rustic countryside cafe. Her social media videos of daily village life drew viewers, some of whom later came to visit. "Once the road opened, more tourists came, and I realized there are just as many opportunities back home as in the city," she said. The changes are reshaping local industries as well. As more visitors arrive, villages along the border are moving beyond simply selling raw produce, instead developing new products and experiences for tourists. In Baoshan Village of Linjiang, blueberries have been grown for more than a decade. Poor mountain roads once made fresh fruit difficult to transport, resulting in losses and limited sales. With better road access, tourists can now enter the village to pick berries, while cold-storage facilities and processing have helped expand the business beyond fresh fruit. Dried blueberries, jam and wine are sold to visitors and shipped nationwide online. The industry now brings the village more than 10 million yuan (about 1.5 million U.S. dollars) in additional annual income, boosting per capita income by over 20,000 yuan. Similarly, in Nanping Township of Helong, six border villages have joined forces to develop local specialties with tourists in mind. Soybean paste, jujube juice and forest honey -- once sold only locally -- are now packaged uniformly as tourism souvenirs and promoted through both livestreaming and in-person sales events. "In the past, we sold whatever we produced. Now we think about what visitors want," said Ji Huadong, a local official. Gao Yun, an official with the Party School of the Jilin Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China, said better connectivity can help turn scattered tourism resources and local specialties into new sources of local growth. "Developing border tourism routes and high-quality tourism products can meet visitors' diverse needs while driving the growth of related industries and the broader regional economy," Gao said. The benefits can extend beyond the economy. As folk traditions and traditional crafts become part of tourism and generate income, local communities have greater incentive to preserve and pass them on, creating a virtuous cycle between cultural preservation and development, experts said. What is happening along the G331 in Jilin is also part of a wider effort to improve transport links in China's border regions. China will advance the high-quality development of transport corridors and support opening-up and development in border regions during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), according to the Ministry of Transport. Over the next five years, China plans to fully connect and upgrade three major highways -- the G219 along the western and southern frontier, the G331 along the northern border and the G228 along the coast -- as part of a "golden outer ring" running along the country's land borders and coastline. Together, they will stretch more than 26,000 km. Ma Jiangbo, deputy director of the China economic research center under the China Institute for Innovation & Development Strategy, said the three corridors will link land and sea routes, turning once-remote border areas into new frontiers of opening-up. "Improved road networks can lower cross-border logistics costs, helping resources from border and coastal regions reach wider markets, and promoting a more balanced industrial layout," Ma added. As dusk settles over the villages along G331, homestays light up. Travelers sit in courtyards sampling local food, while villagers prepare specialties to sell the next day. For places that travelers once merely passed through, the road now offers more reasons to stay -- and gives the communities along it more to build upon. ■
